title: Occasion
short: Written in early 1747 after the drowning of Horace Walpole's cat; published in Dodsley's Collection (1748). Walpole later displayed the vase at Strawberry Hill.
body: Walpole, Gray's friend from Eton and his companion on the Grand Tour, told him that one of his cats had drowned in a large china tub of goldfish. Gray's letter of 1 March 1747 began with mock gravity, asking which of Walpole's cats he was to lament, Zara or Selima (or was it Fatima?), before enclosing the ode. It appeared in Dodsley's Collection of Poems by Several Hands (vol. II, 1748). Walpole later had the first stanza inscribed on the pedestal of the tub at Strawberry Hill. The poem is a mock-heroic: the high style of classical and Miltonic poetry applied to a household accident, with a moral for young women at the end.

anchor: Where China's gayest art had dyed
title: China's gayest art ... azure flowers
short: The vase is Chinese blue-and-white porcelain, a fashionable luxury; its painted flowers 'blow' (bloom) for ever.
body: Chinese export porcelain was a mark of taste in eighteenth-century houses, and contemporary satire often linked it with female vanity. Bradshaw and Tovey cite Lady Mary Wortley Montagu's Town Eclogues for the 'azure' china, and Lonsdale cites Gay's The Toilette and Tickell's Kensington Garden. Johnson, in his Life of Gray, singled out 'the azure flowers that blow' as an example of a rhyme resolutely forced, since the words add nothing; Bradshaw reads 'that blow' as 'that are blowing on it', so that the painted flowers seem to be in full bloom.

title: Selima
short: Walpole's tabby; the name, from Rowe's tragedy Tamerlane (1702), sounds suitably oriental and heroic.
body: Gray's letter pretended uncertainty whether the dead cat was Zara or Selima, adding 'or Fatima'. Lonsdale notes that Selima is a heroine in Nicholas Rowe's Tamerlane. 'Demurest of the tabby kind', 'pensive' and 'reclin'd', she is presented as a young lady of fashion; the gazing on 'the lake below' recalls Milton's Eve admiring her reflection in a lake (Paradise Lost IV.456-469), a parallel the editors note, and so introduces the theme of vanity.

anchor: Her conscious tail her joy declar'd
title: conscious tail ... purr'd applause
short: 'Conscious' means knowing, aware, as if the tail itself shares her pleasure; the stanza is a mirror scene of feline narcissism.
body: The tail is 'conscious' in the eighteenth-century sense of sharing knowledge or feeling (Latin conscius). The blazon of the cat's beauty (round face, snowy beard, velvet paws, tortoiseshell coat, jet ears, emerald eyes) parodies the catalogue of a lady's charms in love poetry. She sees her reflection and 'purr'd applause', applauding herself. The double perspective is Gray's main comic device: every phrase is accurate about a cat and also about a vain young woman.

title: Two angel forms ... The Genii of the stream
short: The goldfish are mock-heroically 'angel forms' and 'Genii', the guardian spirits of the stream.
body: In classical belief a genius loci guarded each place, and Lonsdale cites Milton's 'Il Penseroso' ('th'unseen Genius of the Wood') and Matthew Green's The Grotto. The goldfish become divinities of the tub, and their 'scaly armour' turns them into epic warriors. The elevation prepares for the fall: the cat reaches for what she takes to be prey, but the fish are, in the poem's mythology, protected beings.

title: Their scaly armour's Tyrian hue
short: The fish's colour is described as Tyrian purple through which gold gleams: the royal dye of Tyre, and a hint of gold that tempts.
body: Tyrian purple, made from the murex shellfish at Tyre, was the colour of Roman imperial robes, so the fish are royal as well as martial. Lonsdale cites Dryden's Aeneid (xi, 'A Robe of Tyrian Dye') and Pope's Windsor-Forest (ll. 142, 144). The 'golden gleam' introduces the word that will matter at the end: 'gold' rhymes through the poem as the lure of riches, joined in stanza 4 with the cat's appetite for fish.

title: The hapless nymph
short: Calling a cat a 'nymph' fuses animal and young woman; Johnson complained that it did violence to language and sense.
body: In his Life of Gray Johnson objected that Selima is called a nymph 'with some violence both to language and sense', though he admitted that the device paid off in the couplet that follows. 'Hapless' (unlucky) is a stock epic epithet. Lonsdale lists Milton's Eve, Virgil's Camilla, Gay's The Toilette and Ovid's Daphne among the echoes in the portrait of Selima. 'Nymph' was the regular eighteenth-century term for a young lady in polite verse, as in Pope's Rape of the Lock, which the whole poem echoes in its mock-epic treatment of trivial events.

anchor: What female heart can gold despise
title: What female heart can gold despise? / What Cat's averse to fish?
short: The poem's central joke: two parallel questions, one true of women, one of cats; Johnson admitted the first applies to the nymph and the second to the cat.
body: Johnson observed that the first line relates only to the nymph and the second only to the cat, and he thought the device well used. The couplet makes explicit the double allegory: Selima's desire is both natural appetite and avarice. The satire on women's love of gold and finery was conventional (editors cite Addison's Spectator No. 15, which moralises Virgil's Camilla as a type of female love of show), and modern readers may find it dated or misogynistic, though the poem's tone is genial. 'Gold' and 'fish' are united in the goldfish themselves.

title: Presumptuous maid!
short: A mock-solemn apostrophe like Pope's 'Presumptuous Man!' in An Essay on Man; she does not know 'the gulf between'.
body: Lonsdale compares Pope's Essay on Man (I.35), where human presumption in questioning God's order is rebuked. The 'gulf between' is both the physical gap between the vase's rim and the fish and, in the heightened style, the abyss that separates mortals from forbidden objects. The stanza moves quickly: 'Again she stretch'd, again she bent', and then the parenthesis of 'Malignant Fate' smiling, before 'She tumbled headlong in'.

anchor: Malignant Fate sat by, and smil'd
title: Malignant Fate sat by, and smil'd
short: In mock-epic fashion, a goddess of Fate watches and enjoys the fall; the parenthesis is the narrator's ironic aside.
body: Classical epic often shows the gods watching mortal disasters, and Pope's Rape of the Lock and Dunciad parody the device. The bracketed line slows the action at the brink, and 'beguil'd' (deceived) in the next line makes the slippery rim itself a tempter. The language ('headlong') recalls the falls of Milton's rebel angels, who are hurled 'headlong flaming' from heaven (Paradise Lost I.45), in keeping with the poem's comic use of Miltonic grandeur.

anchor: Eight times emerging from the flood
title: Eight times emerging from the flood
short: A joke on the proverbial nine lives of a cat: she surfaces eight times and is lost on the ninth.
body: Phelps and later editors explain the allusion to the cat's nine lives. Lonsdale also compares Dryden's translation of Homer, where Thetis rises 'emerging from the deep'. Selima mews 'to every watery God', the pagan deities of the sea, but none responds; the mock-epic catalogue of rescuers in the next line confirms the absence. The numerical precision is part of the comedy, since it treats folk superstition as if it were a law of nature, and it makes the drowning seem fated from the start.

anchor: No Dolphin came, no Nereid stirr'd
title: No Dolphin came, no Nereid stirr'd
short: Classical rescuers fail her: no dolphin like the one that saved the poet Arion, no Nereid (sea-nymph); nor did the servants Tom and Susan hear.
body: Herodotus tells how the singer Arion, thrown overboard by sailors, was carried ashore by a dolphin charmed by his music; the Nereids, daughters of Nereus, were sea-nymphs who helped mariners. Lonsdale also cites Sabrina rising to help the Lady in Milton's Comus. The descent from myth to the domestic 'cruel Tom' and 'Susan', generic servants' names, is the bathos of the mock-heroic. The manuscripts and first edition read 'Harry' for 'Susan'.

title: A favourite has no friend!
short: A courtly maxim: those who enjoy a patron's favour are envied, not helped; the Walpole manuscript and 1748 text read 'What favourite has a friend?'
body: The line applies to the pampered pet, whom the servants have no reason to rescue, and also to court favourites, a topical point when the poem's recipient was the son of the former prime minister Sir Robert Walpole. Johnson called it 'a melancholy truth'. The thomasgray.org notes record that the Walpole manuscript and Dodsley's 1748 text have the rhetorical question 'What favourite has a friend?'; Gray later made it a statement.

title: Nor all that glisters gold
short: The moral echoes the proverb 'All that glisters is not gold' (as in The Merchant of Venice); Johnson objected that it does not fit the story.
body: The final stanza addresses 'ye beauties': one false step cannot be undone, so be 'with caution bold'. The last line turns the proverb familiar from Shakespeare's casket scene (Merchant of Venice II.vii.65) and from Chaucer, Spenser and Dryden's Hind and the Panther, all cited by editors. Johnson objected that the poem ends in a pointed sentence unrelated to its purpose: if what glistered had been gold, the cat would still have drowned. Defenders reply that the moral is meant as a comic misfit, part of the mock-solemn manner, and some readers hear in 'false step' a sly sexual warning.

title: Form
short: Seven six-line stanzas rhyming aabccb, with two tetrameter lines and a trimeter, a light lyric form that suits the mock-ode.
body: The stanza (aabccb, lines of 8, 8, 6 syllables twice) is a common lyric sixain, a form of tail-rhyme stanza; Gray calls the poem an ode, but it is closer to a Horatian or comic ode than the Pindaric odes he wrote later. Each short third and sixth line gives a snap that the poet uses for the stanza's point, most famously 'What Cat's averse to fish?' and 'A favourite has no friend!'. The structure is narrative: scene, reflection, temptation, fall, drowning, and a moral.
